title: SRE standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Runbooks, and Incident Reviews
author: Ari Chen
content:
Summary

This document defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards for service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning guidance, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling recommendations, and runbook templates. The goal is to ensure consistent reliability practices across teams, enable predictable capacity, and create a repeatable incident response and postmortem process.

Scope

- Applies to all customer-facing inference services (hosted API, dedicated pools) and critical control-plane services (routing, billing, auth).
- Does not replace team-specific runbooks; instead provides the standard expected format, ownership, and escalation paths.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Overview

SLOs quantify expected service behavior and create operationally actionable error budgets. Each service must define at least one availability SLO and one latency SLO where applicable. SLOs are reviewed quarterly and after any major architecture change or incident.

Required SLO metadata (per service)

- SLO name: short identifier (e.g., "hosted-api.v1.availability").
- SLI definition: measurement and instruments (Prometheus metric or tracing span), aggregation window, and labels used.
- Target: percentage or latency (e.g., 99.95% availability; p95 latency < 200ms for text-generate token response).
- Measurement window: rolling 30-day and 90-day windows required.
- Error budget policy: actions when X% of budget is consumed (see table).
- Owner: primary oncall and product owner contact.

SLO examples (template table)

Service | SLI | Target | Measurement window | Owner
------- | --- | ------ | ------------------ | -----
hosted-api.v1 | Successful request rate (200/2xx) | 99.95% | 30d rolling | inference-team
hosted-api.v1-latency | p95 request-response < 250ms | p95 < 250ms | 30d rolling | inference-team
dedicated-routing | p99 RPC latency | p99 < 100ms | 30d rolling | routing-service-team

Error budget policies (recommended)

- Minor consumption (<= 25% of budget in window): document and monitor; no constraint on feature launches.
- Moderate consumption (25-50%): suspend non-critical experiments and feature launches; schedule a reliability review within 7 days.
- High consumption (50-100%): freeze launches and require a rollback plan for any recent changes; high-priority reliability initiative and weekly progress reports until budget is restored.
- Exhausted budget (>100%): emergency remediation; initiate SRE lead and product-level incident review; require approval for any production changes until budget is restored.

Measurement and tooling

- SLIs must be instrumented in Prometheus (primary) and emitted as tracing spans for correlation. For client-facing APIs use the request_count{status_class=~"2.."} and request_duration_seconds buckets.
- All SLO dashboards should live in Grafana under folder: "SRE / SLOs / <service>".
- Daily error budget burn reports are produced automatically and pushed to the SRE Slack channel #sre-burn-reports.

2) Capacity planning

Principles

- Plan for peak-expected load plus a safety margin: baseline capacity = 2x observed p95 peak for CPU/scheduled throughput and 1.5x for GPU token throughput unless otherwise justified.
- Optimize for cost while meeting latency SLOs: use batching and KV caching to reduce per-token load.
- Maintain a short-term buffer (hot spare) to handle 10% unexpected spike and a medium-term plan to add capacity for forecasted growth.

Quarterly capacity checklist

1. Review last quarter's utilization (cluster, GPU, mem, network) and SLO trends.
2. Update 12-month forecast using product signals: trial signups, deployment rollouts, marketing campaigns.
3. Validate autoscaling policies with chaos-sim tests (see runbook).
4. Schedule reserved capacity procurement for Dedicated pools 60 days ahead of expected need.

Autoscaling and burst policies

- For hosted API: target CPU utilization 55-70% for worker fleets; scale aggressively for latency-sensitive routes.
- For dedicated GPU pools: reserve a minimum commit level and allow burst capacity up to 1.5x with preemption policies.
- Use predictive autoscaling for predictable diurnal patterns; fall back to reactive scaling for sudden spikes.

3) Reliability initiatives and improvement process

Initiative lifecycle

- Propose: Team submits initiative RFC with hypothesis, metrics to improve, and expected ROI.
- Prioritize: SRE council evaluates against tech debt, customer impact, and cost.
- Execute: timeboxed work with a success criteria and measurement plan.
- Close: publish outcomes and update runbooks/SLOs.

Standard initiative types

- Observability improvements (missing SLIs, alert tuning).
- Capacity optimizations (batching, caching, quantization).
- Architectural resilience (redundancy, fallbacks, degraded-mode).
- Automation (deploy safety gates, rollout automation).

4) Incident review and postmortem standards

Goals

- Learn: technical root causes and process failures.
- Fix: actionable remediation with owners and dates.
- Communicate: clear summary for stakeholders.

Postmortem template (required fields)

- Incident ID and timestamp
- Summary (one-paragraph customer-facing)
- Impact (SLOs affected, customers, duration)
- Timeline (bullet list with timestamps)
- Root cause analysis (technical + process)
- Action items (owner, due date, verification criteria)
- Severity and learning classification
- Follow-up review date

Standards

- Postmortems must be published within 7 calendar days and include a clear remediation plan.
- Severity levels: Sev1 (customer-visible outage affecting >1% traffic), Sev2 (partial degradation), Sev3 (single-customer or internal).
- Blameless language required; focus on system/process improvements.

5) Operational tooling and dashboards

Required tooling

- Metrics: Prometheus + Grafana for SLO dashboards and alerting.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry collected to Jaeger/Tempo for request flow analysis.
- Logs: centralized ELK/Cloud-native logging with retention policies per data classification.
- Alerting: Alertmanager rules must map to runbooks (see template) and include runbook links in the alert payload.
- ChatOps: SRE Slack channels with integrations for PagerDuty incidents and automated burn reports.

Alerting guidance

- Follow the 9/90 rule: aim for 9 meaningful alerts per team per week and investigate if a team receives more than 20.
- All high-priority alerts must page the oncall with runbook link and required context (service, SLO impact, recent deploys).

6) Runbooks and playbooks

Runbook format (required)

- Title: service + symptom (e.g., "hosted-api: elevated 5xx rate")
- Pager escalation path: first oncall -> secondary -> SRE oncall -> engineering manager -> product owner (contact details omitted).
- Symptoms and quick checks: list of top-5 immediate checks with exact CLI/queries.
- Mitigation steps (1..n): numbered, reversible, lowest-impact first.
- Full remediation: detailed steps to restore service.
- Post-incident steps: who updates the runbook, and how to close the loop.

Runbook example (excerpt)

Title: hosted-api: elevated 5xx rate
Pager: pagerduty -> #sre-incidents
Quick checks:
1. Check Grafana SLO dashboard: hosted-api availability and 5xx rate.
2. Run: kubectl -n hosted-api get pods -o wide | grep CrashLoopBackOff
3. Query: Prometheus: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="hosted-api",status=~"5.."}[5m])) by (route)
Mitigations:
1. If a single route is failing, disable route in router config (CLI): rctl disable-route --service hosted-api --route /v1/experimental
2. If pod OOMs, scale up replica count by +30% and investigate memory regression.
3. If downstream dependency (model server) times out, divert traffic to fallback model variant (routing policy: degrade -> lightweight-model-v2).

Validation and runbook ownership

- Every runbook must have an owner and be reviewed quarterly.
- Runbooks should include verifiable commands and a minimal checklist to determine success.

8) Ownership, escalation, and governance

- Service owners are responsible for SLO definitions and runbook correctness.
- SRE oncall owns incident coordination and enforcing error budget policies.
- The SRE council meets monthly to review error budget health, capacity forecasts, and open reliability initiatives.

Appendix: common CLI commands and queries

- Prometheus example: curl -G "https://prometheus.internal/api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=rate(http_requests_total{service="hosted-api",status=~"5.."}[5m])'
- Grafana folder path: SRE / SLOs / hosted-api
- Quick kubectl: kubectl -n hosted-api get pods -l app=hosted-api -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CPU:.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.cpu,MEM:.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.memory
